Just got a new ISP (Time Warner Cable; only one who services my building) yesterday. I started downloading a game on Steam, and it was going at 5 MB/s. 10 minutes later it was going at under 300 kB/s. Switched region to Boston, and again it was going at up to 5.3 MB/sec, and about 10 minutes later slowed down. Same deal in Chicago, and then Columbus. Looked at the graphs for this, and there's about a 1 second gap/lost connection when switching to slow mode.

Called them today and their response was "oh well we can send a tech over for a fee," which I doubt will do anything since the tech will run a speed test or look at the initial connection speed and say it's fine.

What's the best way to document this and confront them about it? I doubt it's just Steam that has the problem.

Thanks.
My ISP is throttling any connections after about 10 minutes. How do I confront them about this?

So, as I've understood it what happens is that your computer requests the download, and chooses it's location. C:\Program Files....<snipped>\Steam\

As your computer completes the start of the download (pretty quickly, like choosing the location), the request to the Steam server is initialized. Then packets from the Steam server start their way. Numbered, and on different paths - Called packet switching, which is the fundamental idea of data packets traversing any network large or small.

So this is where the slowdown happens. The download 'settles' a little, and that is where you notice it. (and 10m to 5m is a huge difference)

Another big difference is UDP packets and TCP packets. UDP packets are used for music, movies, and cause a lot of lag and dropped packets, because they can be dropped. Not all the packets are needed to complete the task.

TCP packets (like a video game file) ALL are needed, so if one gets lost, or is dropped, a resend is needed' adding to the time and lowering the download speed.
